questions.question: Q: Name the main stages of the food supply chain from farm to fork.

points.text: Primary production (farming/fishing), processing and manufacturing, distribution and logistics, retail, and food service/consumption.

questions.question: Q: What is the cold chain and why is it important?

points.text: The cold chain is the system of refrigerated transport and storage that keeps perishable foods at safe temperatures throughout the supply chain. A break in the cold chain can cause bacterial growth, food safety issues, and waste.

questions.question: Q: What are the 'Big Four' UK supermarkets?

points.text: Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, and Morrisons. Discounters Aldi and Lidl have significantly grown their market share in recent years.

questions.question: Q: Give three factors that affect food prices.

points.text: Production costs (feed, fuel, labour), weather and harvest yields, global supply and demand, transport costs, government policies (subsidies, tariffs, import duties), and currency exchange rates (any three).

questions.question: Q: What is aquaculture and why is it growing?

points.text: Aquaculture is fish farming — breeding and harvesting fish in controlled environments. It is growing because wild fish stocks are declining due to overfishing, and aquaculture provides a more sustainable and reliable supply.

questions.question: Q: Name three consumer trends currently shaping the food industry.

points.text: Demand for convenience (ready meals, delivery apps), plant-based and vegan products, sustainable and ethically sourced food, online grocery shopping, and clean label/fewer additives (any three).

questions.question: Q: Why is the food industry described as the largest UK manufacturing sector?

points.text: It employs the most people of any manufacturing sector (over 400,000), contributes over £28 billion to the economy annually, and processes the raw materials from the UK's significant agricultural sector.

questions.question: Q: How does the food industry impact the environment?

points.text: Through greenhouse gas emissions (livestock, transport, processing), water usage and pollution, deforestation for farmland, packaging waste, food waste at all stages of the supply chain, and energy consumption in manufacturing and cold storage.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Food travels through several stages from farm to fork. Primary production involves farming (arable crops, livestock, dairy) and fishing or aquaculture, where raw food materials are produced. Processing and manufacturing transforms these raw materials: milling wheat into flour, pasteurising milk, and manufacturing products like bread, cheese, and ready meals. This stage adds value, extends shelf life, and creates convenience products. Distribution and logistics transport food from manufacturers to retailers using road, rail, and sea freight. The cold chain — refrigerated transport and storage — ensures perishable foods remain safe throughout. Retail includes supermarkets, convenience stores, and increasingly online platforms that sell food to consumers. Food service (restaurants, takeaways, catering) prepares and serves food directly. Each stage adds cost, processing, and environmental impact. A major environmental impact is greenhouse gas emissions: livestock farming produces methane, a gas 25 times more potent than CO2; food transport and cold chain logistics consume fossil fuels; and food processing factories use significant energy. The food industry contributes approximately 25–30% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Addressing this requires reduced meat consumption, improved farming efficiency, shorter supply chains, renewable energy in processing, and reduced food waste at all stages.
